topics.title: Accounting ratios: meaning, objectives, advantages and limitations

learn.hook: ₹50 lakh profit – good or bad? It depends on whether sales were ₹1 crore or ₹100 crore. Ratios turn raw numbers into meaning.
points: An accounting ratio is an arithmetical relationship between two related accounting figures. It may be expressed as a pure ratio (2:1), a percentage (25%), times (6 times) or a fraction.
Objectives: know the operational efficiency, liquidity, solvency and profitability of the business, and make inter-firm and intra-firm comparisons.
Advantages: helps judge efficiency of decisions, simplifies complex figures, helps comparative analysis, identifies problem areas, helps in SWOT analysis, and aids planning and forecasting.

Limitations: depends on the limitations of accounting data; ignores price-level changes and qualitative factors; may be affected by window dressing; different accounting policies reduce comparability; there is no universally accepted standard ratio.

example.q: A company has current assets ₹3,00,000 and current liabilities ₹1,50,000. Express their relationship in three forms.
steps: Times: current assets are 2 times current liabilities.

learn.reallife: Bank loan officers in India look at a handful of ratios – current ratio, debt-equity, interest coverage – before sanctioning a business loan.

topics.title: Types of ratios and liquidity ratios

learn.hook: Can the company pay its bills next month? Two quick ratios answer that – the current ratio and the quick ratio.
points: Traditional classification: Statement of Profit and Loss ratios (e.g. gross profit ratio), Balance Sheet ratios (e.g. current ratio, debt-equity), and Composite ratios using both (e.g. trade receivables turnover, return on investment).
Functional classification: liquidity, solvency, activity (turnover) and profitability ratios.
Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities. A ratio of 2:1 is traditionally considered safe.
Quick (liquid) ratio = Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities, where Quick assets = Current assets − Inventories − Prepaid expenses. 1:1 is considered ideal.
Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities. If CR = r and WC is known: CL = WC ÷ (r − 1), CA = CL × r.

example.q: Inventories ₹1,00,000; trade receivables ₹1,20,000; cash ₹60,000; prepaid expenses ₹20,000; current liabilities ₹1,50,000. Find current and quick ratios.

learn.reallife: Suppliers to large retailers like DMart check liquidity ratios before extending long credit periods.

topics.title: Debt-equity and debt to capital employed

learn.hook: How much of the company is funded by lenders versus owners? Too much debt, and a bad year can sink it.
points: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debts ÷ Shareholders' funds (equity). Long-term debts = Long-term borrowings + Long-term provisions.
Shareholders' funds = Share capital + Reserves and surplus (+ money received against share warrants). Alternatively: Non-current assets + Working capital − Non-current liabilities.
A lower debt-equity ratio means more security for lenders; a common safe norm is 2 : 1.
Debt to capital employed ratio = Long-term debts ÷ Capital employed, where Capital employed = Long-term debts + Shareholders' funds (or Non-current assets + Working capital).

example.q: Share capital ₹8,00,000; reserves and surplus ₹2,00,000; long-term borrowings (debentures) ₹5,00,000. Find debt-equity and debt to capital employed ratios.

learn.reallife: RBI and banks watch the leverage of big Indian conglomerates closely; a high debt-equity ratio can trigger rating downgrades.

topics.title: Proprietary, total assets to debt and interest coverage ratios

learn.hook: Owners' share of the assets, assets backing each rupee of debt, and how many times profit covers interest – three more solvency checks.
points: Proprietary ratio = Shareholders' funds ÷ Total assets. A higher ratio means owners finance more of the assets.
Total assets to debt ratio = Total assets ÷ Long-term debts. A higher ratio means lenders are better protected.
Interest coverage ratio = Net profit before interest and tax ÷ Interest on long-term debt. It shows how many times interest is covered by profit.
Total assets here are taken as shown in the balance sheet (excluding fictitious items).

example.q: Total assets ₹20,00,000; shareholders' funds ₹10,00,000; 10% debentures ₹5,00,000; profit before interest and tax ₹3,00,000. Compute the three ratios.

learn.reallife: Credit analysts reviewing Indian infrastructure companies obsess over interest coverage – below 1.5 times rings alarm bells.

learn.hook: A sweet shop that sells its stock every few days is healthier than one whose laddoos sit for weeks. Inventory turnover measures that speed.
points: Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of revenue from operations ÷ Average inventory.
Average inventory = (Opening inventory + Closing inventory) ÷ 2.
Cost of revenue from operations = Revenue from operations − Gross profit, or = Opening inventory + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing inventory.
If gross profit is given on cost (e.g. 25% on cost), cost of revenue = Revenue × 100 ÷ (100 + 25). If given on revenue, cost = Revenue × (100 − GP%) ÷ 100.
A higher ratio generally means efficient inventory management; too high may mean stock-outs.

topics.title: Trade receivables and trade payables turnover

learn.hook: Customers pay you in 73 days but you pay suppliers in 60. That gap can squeeze your cash – turnover ratios reveal it.
points: Trade receivables turnover = Net credit revenue from operations ÷ Average trade receivables. Trade receivables = Debtors + Bills receivable (before deducting provision for doubtful debts).
Trade payables turnover = Net credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables. Trade payables = Creditors + Bills payable.
Average collection period = 365 days (or 12 months) ÷ Trade receivables turnover.
Average payment period = 365 days (or 12 months) ÷ Trade payables turnover.
Higher receivables turnover = faster collection; higher payables turnover = faster payment to suppliers.

example.q: Credit revenue ₹7,50,000; trade receivables: opening ₹1,20,000, closing ₹1,80,000. Find turnover and average collection period.

learn.reallife: Small suppliers to large companies in India often complain about long payment periods – which is why the MSME Act sets limits on delayed payments.

topics.title: Net assets, fixed assets and working capital turnover

learn.hook: How many rupees of sales does each rupee of capital generate? Three turnover ratios measure how hard the company's money is working.
points: Net assets (capital employed) turnover = Revenue from operations ÷ Capital employed.
Fixed assets turnover = Revenue from operations ÷ Net fixed assets (after depreciation).
Working capital turnover = Revenue from operations ÷ Working capital (current assets − current liabilities).
Higher ratios generally indicate better use of resources.

topics.title: Gross profit ratio, operating ratio and operating profit ratio

learn.hook: Out of every ₹100 of sales, how much is left after the cost of goods – and after running the business? These three ratios tell you.
points: Gross profit ratio = Gross profit ÷ Net revenue from operations × 100. Net revenue = revenue − returns.

Operating ratio = (Cost of revenue from operations + Operating expenses) ÷ Net revenue from operations × 100. Operating expenses include office and administration, selling and distribution, employee benefits and depreciation.
Operating profit ratio = Operating profit ÷ Net revenue from operations × 100, where operating profit = revenue − operating cost.
Operating profit ratio = 100 − Operating ratio.
Non-operating items (interest on investments, loss by fire, profit on sale of assets) are excluded from operating ratios.

example.q: Sales ₹10,50,000; returns ₹50,000; cost of revenue ₹7,00,000; operating expenses ₹1,00,000. Compute the three ratios.

topics.title: Net profit ratio and return on investment

learn.hook: The bottom line and the big question: for every ₹100 invested, how much does the business earn?
points: Net profit ratio = Net profit ÷ Revenue from operations × 100. It can be based on profit before tax or profit after tax.
Return on investment (ROI), or return on capital employed = Profit before interest and tax ÷ Capital employed × 100.
PBIT = Profit before tax + interest on long-term debt (finance costs on long-term borrowings).
Capital employed = Shareholders' funds + Long-term debts (or Non-current assets + Working capital).
ROI judges overall efficiency; compare it with the cost of borrowing to decide whether more debt helps owners.

learn.reallife: Investors comparing Indian banks and IT majors often look first at ROI/ROCE – it shows who uses capital best.

topics.title: Ratio applications: effects of transactions and missing figures

learn.hook: Board-exam favourite: 'Will paying a creditor raise or lower the current ratio?' Master the logic, not just the formula.
points: When current ratio > 1: an equal decrease in CA and CL (e.g. paying a creditor) INCREASES the ratio; an equal increase (e.g. buying goods on credit) DECREASES it.
Transactions within current assets (e.g. collecting from debtors) do not change the current ratio; a current asset used for a non-current asset (buying machinery for cash) reduces it.
Debt-equity: issue of equity shares or conversion of debentures into shares reduces it; issue of debentures for cash increases it.
Missing figures: use the ratio definitions as equations, e.g. CR 2.5, QR 1.5, CL ₹80,000 → CA ₹2,00,000, quick assets ₹1,20,000, inventory ₹80,000 (if no prepaid expenses).
Comprehensive questions: compute several ratios from one set of statements – always identify CA, CL, equity, long-term debt and capital employed first.

example.q: Current ratio is 2 : 1 (CA ₹2,00,000, CL ₹1,00,000). Creditors of ₹50,000 are paid. New ratio?

learn.reallife: Finance managers sometimes time payments to suppliers before year-end to improve the reported current ratio – one reason analysts watch for window dressing.
